title: Understanding California's Fair Employment and Housing Act for Buyers and Sellers
content_html:
What the Fair Employment and Housing Act Covers in Real Estate

California's Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) is best known for workplace protections, but it also contains the state's primary fair housing law, which applies directly to real estate transactions — including the sale, rental, and financing of housing. The housing provisions of FEHA make it unlawful to discriminate in housing-related transactions based on a list of protected characteristics set out in the California Government Code.[1]

For buyers and sellers in Temecula Valley, Murrieta, and Menifee, understanding these protections isn't just a compliance exercise — it shapes how listings are marketed, how offers are evaluated, and how everyone involved in a transaction is expected to behave from the first showing through closing.

Who and What Is Protected

California's fair housing statute lists specific protected characteristics, including race, color, religion, sex, gender, gender identity and expression, sexual orientation, marital status, national origin, ancestry, familial status, source of income, disability, and genetic information, among others identified in the statute.[1] This protection is broader in some respects than the federal Fair Housing Act, which covers a narrower list of classes.

These protections apply across the full housing transaction process — not only to whether a seller will accept an offer, but to advertising, financing terms, appraisal practices, and the terms and conditions offered to different buyers or tenants.

What This Means for Sellers

Sellers and their agents cannot use a prospective buyer's membership in a protected class as a factor in deciding whether to sell, what price or terms to offer, or how to market a property. This includes:

  • Advertising language: Marketing copy and listing descriptions should avoid any language that expresses a preference for or against buyers based on a protected characteristic.
  • Evaluating offers: When multiple offers come in, the terms of the offer — price, contingencies, financing strength, closing timeline — are the legitimate basis for comparison, not assumptions about who is submitting them.
  • Showings and access: All interested, qualified buyers should have equal opportunity to view a property and submit an offer.

Sellers sometimes ask whether they can express a personal preference about who buys their home — for example, hoping a "young family" moves in. Statements like this, even if well-intentioned, can raise fair housing concerns because they reference a protected characteristic (familial status) as a stated preference. A good practice is to let an agent handle communications about a listing and keep personal preferences about a hypothetical buyer out of any public-facing marketing or conversations with other agents.

What This Means for Buyers

Buyers are protected from discriminatory treatment at every stage of a transaction, including:

  • Being steered toward or away from certain neighborhoods based on a protected characteristic (a practice often referred to as "steering").
  • Being offered different loan terms, down payment requirements, or financing guidance based on a protected characteristic.
  • Being discouraged from viewing or bidding on a property that is otherwise within their stated price range and criteria.
  • Having an appraisal or home valuation be influenced by assumptions connected to a protected characteristic.

If a buyer believes they were treated differently because of a protected characteristic — denied a showing, given inconsistent information compared with other buyers, or steered toward specific areas — that experience is worth documenting and raising with a real estate professional or, if appropriate, with the appropriate state agency.

Source of Income and Disability-Related Protections

Two categories of protection are worth calling out specifically because they come up often in everyday transactions and rentals:

Source of income protection means that housing providers generally cannot refuse to consider an otherwise qualified applicant or buyer simply because part or all of their income comes from a lawful source such as a housing voucher, child support, or disability benefits, as defined under the statute.[1]

Disability-related protections include the right to request reasonable accommodations and modifications to a dwelling or to the terms of a housing transaction, so that a person with a disability has an equal opportunity to use and enjoy a home. These requests are evaluated individually, and what counts as "reasonable" depends on the specific circumstances.

How FEHA Housing Complaints Are Handled

The California Civil Rights Department (formerly the Department of Fair Employment and Housing) is the state agency responsible for receiving and investigating housing discrimination complaints under FEHA. The statute sets out the state's framework for enforcement, investigation, and the types of relief available, including administrative and civil remedies.[1] A person who believes they experienced housing discrimination can file a complaint with the department, and in some circumstances may also have the option to pursue a civil action.

Because the specific procedures, timelines, and available remedies can be detailed and fact-specific, anyone who believes they've experienced housing discrimination should review the statute directly or consult an attorney rather than relying on general summaries — including this one.

How This Shows Up in Everyday Transactions

In practice, fair housing compliance is mostly about consistency and documentation. Agents and sellers who treat every buyer the same way — same information, same access to showings, same process for submitting and evaluating offers — are far less likely to run into a fair housing issue than those who make case-by-case judgment calls based on assumptions about who a buyer is. The same logic applies to landlords and property managers handling rental applications, and to lenders evaluating loan applications.

If you're a buyer working through how to put together a competitive offer, it helps to know that your offer will — and should — be evaluated on its merits: price, terms, financing, and timeline. If you're a seller preparing to list, your agent should be able to walk you through how offers get compared and documented so the process is defensible and fair to everyone involved.

A Few Practical Takeaways

  • Protected characteristics should never factor into pricing, marketing, showing access, or offer evaluation.
  • Source-of-income protections mean qualified buyers and tenants using vouchers or other lawful income sources generally cannot be turned away for that reason alone.
  • Reasonable accommodation and modification requests related to a disability are handled individually and should be discussed with your agent or housing provider.
  • Concerns about discriminatory treatment should be documented and can be raised with the California Civil Rights Department.
  • When in doubt, consistency is the safest practice — apply the same process and standards to every buyer, seller, tenant, or applicant.

About George Khazanovskiy

George Khazanovskiy is a Temecula Valley real estate agent (DRE #02034120) with Allison James Estates & Homes. Reach George at 619-277-2766 or askgeorgek@gmail.com.

mainEntity.name: Does California's fair housing law cover more than the federal Fair Housing Act?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. California's Fair Employment and Housing Act includes additional protected characteristics beyond those covered by the federal Fair Housing Act, such as source of income and certain additional categories defined under state law.

mainEntity.name: Can a seller say they'd prefer a certain type of buyer for their home?

acceptedAnswer.text: Expressing a preference tied to a protected characteristic, even informally, can raise fair housing concerns. It's best to let your agent handle buyer communications and evaluate offers on objective terms.

mainEntity.name: Where do I file a housing discrimination complaint in California?

acceptedAnswer.text: Complaints under FEHA's housing provisions are handled by the California Civil Rights Department. Specific procedures and timelines should be confirmed directly with the department or with an attorney.
